questions.question: A 55-year-old man undergoes a routine colonoscopy. During the procedure, a polyp is discovered. Histological examination reveals serrated architecture, as shown in the image. Which of the following is true about this polyp?

options.B: Predominantly found in the left colon
options.C: Serrated architecture is limited to the surface of the lesions
options.D: Do not require surveillance or follow-up after detection

explanation.text: The above image shows serrations throughout the full length of the glands including crypt base which is suggestive of sessile serrated adenoma which has malignant potential.

Sessile Serrated Adenomas (SSA): Exhibit serrated architecture throughout the full length of the gland while hyperplastic polyps have serrated architecture only in the upper third of the crypt. (Option C) It has malignant potential More commonly located in the right colon. (Option B) Lack typical cytologic features of dysplasia found in other adenomas. Early precursor lesions in the serrated neoplasia pathway.
Associated with BRAF-mutated colorectal carcinomas. Require follow-up surveillance for monitoring changes or growth. (Option D)

questions.question: A 4-year-old girl presents to the OPD with complaints of rectal bleeding and abdominal pain for the past six months. Investigations reveal approximately 40 hamartomatous colon polyps. The biopsy shows cystic spaces with dilated glands filled with mucin and inflammatory debris. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?

explanation.text: The given clinical presentation and investigation findings suggests a possible diagnosis of Juvenile Polyposis Syndrome (JPS). Juvenile polyposis Syndrome Primarily affects children under 5 years old. Autosomal dominant inheritance Can be sporadic or syndromic. Sporadic: Single polyps. Syndromic: 3-100 polyps. Linked to mutations in the SMAD4 and BMPR1A genes, part of the TGF-β signaling pathway.

Pedunculated polyp which is usually less than 3 cm in diameter. Contains cystic spaces filled with mucin and inflammatory debris. Extra-intestinal manifestations include congenital malformations, digital clubbing.

questions.question: A 13-year-old female presents to the OPD due to abdominal pain and blood in stools. On examination, she had pigmented macules on her lips and oral mucosa. Endoscopy reveals multiple large, pedunculated polyps in the small intestine which shows an arborizing pattern of smooth muscle and glands lined by normal epithelium. Which of the following statements is incorrect about this condition? Autosomal dominant disorder Polyps are more common in the colon Increased risk of developing colon, pancreatic, and breast cancers Gain-of-function mutation in STK11 gene

explanation.text: The given clinical scenario and histological findings point towards the diagnosis of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome: Autosomal dominant disorder. (statement 1) Caused by a loss of function mutation in the STK11 gene (statement 4) Presents around 11 years of age.

Characterized by: Gastrointestinal hamartomatous polyps especially in the small intestine (statement 2) Mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation (macules on lips, nostrils, buccal mucosa, and extremities). Polyps are large, pedunculated, and lobulated. Histology - an arborizing pattern of smooth muscle and glands lined by normal epithelium. Significantly increased cancer risk (statement 3) Gastrointestinal tract, pancreas, breasts, gonads, and uterus.
Lifetime cancer risk estimated at 40%

questions.question: A 58-year-old female presents with weight loss, nail changes, alopecia, and skin hyperpigmentation. Colonoscopy reveals multiple hamartomatous polyps in the intestine. Family history is negative for intestinal cancers. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: The clinical presentation and multiple noncancerous polyps in the colon, coupled with a lack of family history of similar symptoms suggests Cronkhite-Canada Syndrome (CCS).

Cronkhite-Canada syndrome Rare, non-hereditary condition Mean age of presentation: >50 years Characterized by: Widespread non cancerous/hamartomatous gastrointestinal polyposis Cutaneous changes - alopecia, hyperpigmentation) Nail dystrophy Polyps: Symptoms: Malabsorption, diarrhea, weight loss Tuberous sclerosis (Option A) is a neurocutaneous disorder resulting from mutations in the TSC1 (hamartin) or TSC2 (tuberin) genes.
Patients exhibit neurological symptoms like seizures, along with skin abnormalities. The syndrome also includes hamartomatous polyps in the intestine.
**Bannayan-Ruvalcaba-Riley Syndrome (Option B):** is a genetic condition characterized by macrocephaly, intestinal hamartomatous polyps and pigmented maculae of the glans penis.

**Cowden syndrome (Option C):** is caused by mutation of PTEN gene on chromosome 10. It is associated with multiple hamartomatous polyps, benign skin tumors like trichilemmoma and an increased risk of breast, thyroid, and endometrial cancers.

questions.question: A 20-year-old man with a family history of colorectal carcinoma presents with chronic abdominal discomfort and occasional rectal bleeding.Upon further evaluation, a mutation in APC gene is identified leading to a diagnosis of Familial Adenomatous Polyposis. Which of the following statement is true regarding FAP?

options.B: 50 % risk of colon cancer if untreated
options.C: Presence of a minimum of 100 polyps
options.D: Congenital atrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium

explanation.text: Classic FAP is characterized by the presence of a minimum of 100 polyps Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP) Autosomal dominant disorder caused by APC gene mutations on chromosome 5 (Option A) Numerous intestinal polyps develop Classic FAP: Diagnosed with at least 100 polyps (Option C) Almost 100% risk of colorectal cancer if untreated (Option B) Commonly develops by 30 years, almost always by 50 years Attenuated FAP (AFAP): Primarily affects the proximal colon Fewer polyps (average <30 polyps) Associated with congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (Option D) Standard treatment: Prophylactic colectomy to prevent colorectal cancer Post-colectomy risks: Cancer at extracolonic sites, including the ampulla of Vater and stomach

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman presents with a history of unexplained weight loss along with multiple sebaceous cysts on her face and scalp. She has a family history of colorectal cancer. Upon further examination, she is found to have a bony lesion on her jaw. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: The clinical findings given suggest Gardner syndrome as a possible diagnosis.

Gardner syndrome An autosomal dominant condition Characterized by colonic polyposis and extracolonic manifestations Due to mutations in APC gene Predisposition to colo-rectal cancer present Extracolonic manifestations include Osteomas (commonly in skull and mandible) Supernumerary teeth Epidermoid cysts Fibromas Thyroid and desmoid tumors Supernumerary teeth Option A) Turcot syndrome: Turcot syndrome can also arise from mutations in APC genes.

But, there is association with brain tumors along with colorectal cancer Option C) Lynch syndrome: AKA HNPCC(hereditary non polyposis colorectal cancer) Autosomal dominant condition due to mutations in MLH 1 and MSH 2 Characterized by increases risk of colorectal cancer, endometrial, ovarian, uterus and Pancreatic cancers Option D) MUTYH Associated Polyposis (MAP) Rare autosomal recessive disorder due to mutations in the MUTYH gene.

Occurs later in life compared to other polyposis syndromes Involves fewer than 100 polyps and individuals with MAP have an increased risk of colorectal cancer. Unlike Gardner syndromes, MAP is not associated with osteomas or epidermoid cysts.

questions.question: A 6 cm polyp is identified in the descending colon during a routine colonoscopy. Histological examination reveals villous architecture with high-grade dysplasia. Based on this scenario, which factors most strongly correlate with the risk of malignancy in colorectal adenomas?

explanation.text: The size of colorectal adenomas is the most critical factor associated with the risk of malignancy. Larger adenomas are most likely to develop into invasive carcinoma Adenomas larger than 4 cm in diameter have nearly a 40% chance of containing invasive cancer.

**Villous architecture (Option A):** Villous adenomas are associated with a higher incidence of cancer than tubular adenomas, but this correlation primarily arises from their larger size rather than their architectural characteristics alone.

**Histologic grade of dysplasia (Option C):** High-grade dysplasia within an individual polyp increases its risk of harboring cancer. However, histologic grade of dysplasia is not the primary factor correlating with the overall risk of malignancy across adenomas.

**Gastrointestinal tract location (Option D):** While certain types of polyps may have preferences for specific locations within the gastrointestinal tract (e.g., sessile serrated lesions are more common in the right colon), location alone is not the strongest predictor of malignancy in colorectal adenomas.

questions.question: A patient underwent genetic testing after being diagnosed with colon cancer. Testing reveals a mutation associated with Hereditary Nonpolyposis Colorectal Cancer (HNPCC). Which of the following genes is defective in this patient?

explanation.text: Hereditary Nonpolyposis Colorectal Cancer (HNPCC), also known as Lynch syndrome, is caused by inherited mutations in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes - MSH2 and MLH1.

**Genes mutation Manifestation MLH1, MSH2 (Option D):** Results in microsatellite instability Causes cluster of cancer: Colorectal, Endometrial, Ovarian, Pancreatic cancers Colon cancer develops at a young age and it usually occurs in the right side SMAD4 and BMPR1 (Option A) Juvenile polyposis syndrome STK11 (Option B) Peutz-Jeghers syndrome APC gene (Option C) Familial Adenomatous Polyposis(FAP), sporadic colon cancer, Gardner syndrome and Turcot syndrome MUTYH (Option C) MUTYH-associated polyposis.

questions.question: A 55-year-old male presents to the clinic with complaints of recurrent abdominal discomfort and changes in bowel habits over the past few months. Further investigation with colonoscopy confirmed the presence of adenocarcinoma. Which of the following factors is most closely associated with this condition?

options.C: High intake of unabsorbable vegetable fiber

explanation.text: High consumption of red meat is associated with increased risk of adenocarcinoma of the colon Factors increasing the risk Factors decreasing the risk Low fiber, high fat diet High intake of red meat and processed meat Increased calorie intake and obesity Family history of colon cancer Personal history of adenomas Smoking and alcohol Inflammatory bowel disease Lynch syndrome FAP Acromegaly Pelvis irradiation Streptococcus bovis septicemia Ureterosigmoidoscopy High fiber diet Intake of fish (omega-3 fatty acids), fruits and vegetables (Vit A, C, E) NSAID use, particularly Aspirin Folic acid Calcium Hormone replacement therapy

questions.question: A 55-year-old female presents with abdominal pain, changes in bowel habits, unintended weight loss. A previous colonoscopy showed a polyp, but a recent one confirmed colorectal adenocarcinoma. Which gene mutations are characteristically associated with development of colorectal adenocarcinoma?

explanation.text: The genes associated with development of colorectal carcinoma are APC, KRAS, SMAD4 and TP53. Adenoma-Carcinoma Sequence: Accounts for up to 80% of sporadic cancers. APC Gene Mutations: Leads to β-catenin accumulation and Wnt pathway activation. "First hit": Sporadic inactivation of APC. "Second hit": Loss of second APC copy KRAS Mutations: Promote growth and prevent apoptosis.
SMAD2 and SMAD4 Mutations: Disrupt TGF-β pathway, causing uncontrolled proliferation. TP53 Mutations: Occur in later stages of tumor progression.

questions.question: A 45-year-old female presents with abdominal pain, changes in bowel habits, and weight loss. Her mother and aunt were diagnosed with endometrial and ovarian cancer in their 50s. A colonoscopy and a biopsy confirm well-differentiated adenocarcinoma. Which genetic pathway is most likely associated with adenocarcinoma in this patient?

explanation.text: The patient's family history of endometrial and ovarian cancer, combined with her well-differentiated adenocarcinoma, suggests Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) which is associated with DNA mismatch repair pathway Lynch syndrome occurs due to germline mutations in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes resulting in microsatellite instability (MSI) Option A) APC/β-catenin pathway: This is commonly associated with the classic adenoma-carcinoma sequence in colorectal adenocarcinoma.

Options B & D): TGF-β signaling pathway and pro-apoptotic protein BAX regulate cell growth, differentiation, and apoptosis. While these signalling pathways are alterations in colorectal cancer, they are not commonly associated with MSI or Lynch syndrome.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common site of metastasis for colon adenocarcinoma?

explanation.text: The liver is the most common site of distant metastasis for colon adenocarcinoma. This is due to the portal venous drainage of the colon, which allows cancer cells to spread easily to the liver. Other sites:Lymph nodes, lungs, and bones can metastasize Prognostic factors Depth of invasion Lymph node metastases.

questions.question: A 60-year-old male presents with abdominal pain, altered bowel habits and 5kg weight loss in one month. A barium enema study showed the following finding. Which of the following statements is true about the patient's condition?

options.A: Presents asweakness due to iron deficiency anemia
options.B: Leads to a napkin-ring constriction and luminal narrowing
options.C: Growth tends to be polypoidal (growth is into the wall of the intestine?)

explanation.text: Distal colorectal carcinoma leads to formation of a napkin ring constriction and luminal narrowing which can be seen as an apple core appearance on barium enema study Proximal adenocarcinoma (masses on the caecum and ascending colon) Grow as polypoidal and exophytic masses which extend along one wall. (Option C) Present with occult anemia, causing late-stage weakness. (Option A) Distal Adenocarcinoma Equally distributed along the colon.

Lesions are annular, causing napkin-ring constrictions and luminal narrowing.(Option B) Barium study - apple core appearance Present early with changes in bowel habits, Hematochezia, cramping, left lower quadrant pain. Cell Composition: Tall columnar cells resembling dysplastic epithelium in adenomas. Mucinous Adenocarcinoma:Contains signet-ring cells producing abundant mucin. They are rare and associated with poor prognosis. (Option D)

questions.question: A 47-year-old male presents with chronic diarrhoea, unintentional weight loss, joint pain, pallor, and generalised weakness. Upper GI endoscopy and biopsy revealed characteristic histopathological findings suggestive of Whipple's disease. Which of the following histopathological features would have led to the diagnosis?

options.A: Foamy macrophages filled with PAS-positive granules
options.B: Villous atrophy and blunting of the small intestinal mucosa
options.C: Lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate in the lamina propria
options.D: Presence of caseating granulomas and acid-fast bacilli

explanation.text: Whipple's disease is a malabsorption problem: Nothing will get absorbed from the intestine, especially fats, leading to Steatorrhea. Whipple’s disease: Feature

questions.question: A 35-year-old female presents with chronic diarrhoea, abdominal bloating, and unintended weight loss. She reports discomfort after consuming gluten-containing foods. Laboratory tests show elevated tissue transglutaminase (tTG) and anti-endomysial antibodies (EMA) levels, prompting a small intestinal biopsy via upper endoscopy. Which of the following combinations of histopathological features will be seen in this condition? Intraepithelial CD8+ T Lymphocytes Crypt hyperplasia Villous atrophy Decreased mitotic activity Inflammatory cell infiltration in lamina propria

explanation.text: The clinical scenario is classic for Celiac disease, an autoimmune disorder triggered by gluten ingestion, confirmed by: Positive anti-tTG and anti-EMA antibodies Small bowel biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis Marsh criteria of celiac disease: Because the antibodies are formed due to consumption of gluten, they first attack the villi of intestine (Villous atrophy) Histopathological features in Celiac disease: Feature Seen in Celiac?

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman presents to the clinic with a history of chronic abdominal pain and diarrhoea, worsening notably after consuming wheat-based foods. Physical examination reveals signs suggestive of malabsorption. Considering celiac disease as a possible diagnosis, which of the following statements regarding its pathogenesis is NOT correct?

options.A: Gliadin peptides in the lamina propria are deamidated by tissue transglutaminase.
options.B: HLA-DR2 or HLA-DR8 significantly influences celiac disease susceptibility.
options.C: Gliadin peptides may induce epithelial cells to express IL-15, activating CD8+ lymphocytes.
options.D: Type 1 diabetes, Sjögren syndrome, and IgA nephropathy are associated with celiac disease.

explanation.text: Celiac disease (aka celiac sprue or gluten-sensitive enteropathy) is an immune-mediated condition triggered by consuming foods containing gluten, such as barley, rye, oats, and wheat. It is influenced by HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8, not HLA-DR2 or HLA-DR8 Gliadin is released when these patient consumes gluten.

Pathogenesis of Celiac disease: Gliadin peptides ↓ Deamidated by Tissue transglutaminase (TTG) enzyme of intestine ↓ IL-15 expression ↓ CD8+ t-lymphocytes activated ↓ Epithelial damage Genetic variations may link celiac disease to other immune disorders, such as type 1 diabetes, thyroiditis, Sjogren syndrome, and IgA nephropathy. (Option D)

questions.question: A 35-year-old female who recently returned from a tropical region presents with persistent diarrhoea, weight loss, fatigue, anaemia, and vitamin deficiencies, along with a small intestine biopsy findings of villous atrophy and chronic mucosal inflammation. Which part of the gastrointestinal tract is typically NOT affected in this condition?

explanation.text: The clinical scenario, with a history of returning from a tropical region and biopsy findings, points towards diagnosing Tropical enteropathy or Environmental enteropathy that does not affect the colon. This disease often occurs after E. coli infection. Tropical sprue: Predominantly affects the small intestine( duodenum, jejunum, and ileum) and presents with Iron deficiency anemia or megaloblastic anemia.
Part of the small intestine Nutrient absorbed Duodenum Iron Jejunum Folic acid Ileum Vitamin B12

questions.question: A 6-month-old infant presents with failure to thrive, chronic diarrhoea, and poor weight gain. A peripheral blood smear revealed a characteristic appearance, as shown in the image below. Biochemical investigations reveal very low levels of triglycerides, cholesterol, and fat-soluble vitamins. Which genetic mutation is most likely responsible for these findings?

explanation.text: The given clinical scenario and peripheral smear findings suggest Abetalipoproteinemia, caused by a mutation in Microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTTP), which is required for the transfer of lipids to nascent apolipoprotein B polypeptide in the endoplasmic reticulum.

Abetalipoproteinemia: Aetiology Mutation in Microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTTP) Presentation Extremely low cholesterol and triglycerides Malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins. Intestine shows lipid vacuoles because of problem in lipid transfer. Biochemical investigation Low triglyceride cholesterol levels Low fat soluble vitamin levels Symptoms Presents in infancy with failure to thrive, diarrhoea, and steatorrhea.
Peripheral smear Presence of acanthocytes -RBCs with peripheral spikes

questions.question: A 4-week-old infant presents with severe watery diarrhoea and failure to thrive since birth. Stool studies are negative for pathogens. A small bowel biopsy shows villous atrophy, cytoplasmic inclusion bodies within enterocytes, and reduction of microvilli on the enterocyte surface. Which of the following statements is true regarding this condition?

options.A: It is characterised by the absence of ganglion cells in the distal part of the colon.
options.B: It is associated with mutations in the MYO5B or STX3 genes.
options.C: Histological findings include villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia.
options.D: It is commonly caused by rotavirus infection, which leads to persistent diarrhoea.

explanation.text: The clinical presentation suggests Microvillous Inclusion Disease (MVID). It is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterised by severe, intractable watery diarrhoea from early infancy. It presents with inclusion bodies and reduction in microvilli. Aetiology: Mutations in the MYO5B or STX3 genes.
**It is characterised by the absence of ganglion cells in the distal part of the colon (Option A):** Seen in Hirschsprung disease.
**Histological findings include villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia (Option C):** Seen in celiac disease or gluten insensitivity.
**It is commonly caused by rotavirus infection, which leads to persistent diarrhoea (Option D):** Stool studies are negative for pathogen in this case.

questions.question: A 28-year-old female presents with foul-smelling, greasy diarrhoea, bloating, and abdominal cramps following a hiking trip in a remote area. Stool microscopy reveals cysts containing motile trophozoites. A duodenal biopsy shows luminal organisms, as shown in the image, without tissue invasion. Based on the clinical presentation and biopsy findings, what is the most likely causative organism?

explanation.text: The scenario is of Giardia lamblia infestation Giardia lamblia: Definition Flagellated protozoan parasite Commonly associated with contaminated water sources. Symptoms Foul-smelling-greasy diarrhoea Bloating Abdominal cramps. Biopsy findings Luminal organisms attached to the intestinal epithelium Blunting of the villi and inflammation without tissue invasion.
**Giardia trophozoites on biopsy are often described as resembling "falling leaves" Cryptosporidium (Option A):** Coccidian parasite Usually present along brush border of the intestine.

**Causes watery diarrhoea, especially in immunocompromised individuals Tropheryma whipplei (Option B):** Causes Whipple's disease Histology: PAS-positive foamy macrophages in the intestinal mucosa Entamoeba histolytica (Option C) Protozoan parasite It causes amoebic ulcer in intestine identified by flask shaped ulcers.
